name: git diff
shortDescription: Show changes between commits, branches, the staging area, and the working directory. This is how you inspect exactly what changed before committing.
detailedDescription:
The `git diff` command shows the exact lines that were added, removed, or modified between two states of your code. By default (with no arguments), it shows the difference between your working directory and the staging area — in other words, what you've changed but not yet staged.

Diffs use a unified format: lines starting with `+` (in green) are additions, lines starting with `-` (in red) are removals, and lines with no prefix are unchanged context. The `@@` markers show line numbers.

There are three primary comparisons:
- **Working directory vs Staging area**: `git diff` (shows unstaged changes)
- **Staging area vs Last commit**: `git diff --staged` (shows what will be committed)
- **Between commits/branches**: `git diff branch1..branch2`

The diff output is the same format used in pull request reviews, making it essential to understand.

parameters.description: Shows unstaged changes: the difference between your working directory and the staging area. If you haven't staged anything, this compares against the last commit.
Shows changes between the staging area and the last commit. This is exactly what `git commit` will record. Both flags are identical; --staged is more intuitive.
Instead of showing line-by-line changes, show a summary: which files changed, how many insertions (+) and deletions (-) occurred. The same format GitHub uses in PRs.
Show only the names of changed files, not the actual changes. Useful for scripting or getting a quick overview.
Compare two specific commits, branches, or tags. For example, `git diff main..feature` shows what's different between the two branches.
Restrict the diff to a specific file or directory. Useful when the full diff is too long.
Show changes at the word level instead of the line level. Much more readable for prose, documentation, or small variable name changes.

examples.title: See what you changed but haven't staged
examples.description: The most common usage. After editing files, see exactly what changed before staging.

examples.title: Review staged changes before committing
examples.description: After staging files, verify exactly what will go into the commit. This is your last chance to catch mistakes.
examples.code:
git add .
git diff --staged

# Shows all changes that are staged and ready to commit

examples.title: Compare two branches
examples.description: See all the differences between your feature branch and main. This is essentially what a PR review shows.
examples.code:
git diff main..feature-login

# Or just see the file names that differ:
git diff main..feature-login --name-only

# Or a summary with insertions/deletions:
git diff main..feature-login --stat

examples.title: Diff a specific file
examples.description: When the diff is too long, focus on a single file.
examples.code:
git diff -- src/auth/login.js
git diff --staged -- src/auth/login.js

examples.title: Compare with a specific commit
examples.description: See all changes since a particular commit. Useful for reviewing what happened during a sprint or since a release.
examples.code:
# Changes since commit a1b2c3d:
git diff a1b2c3d

# Changes between two specific commits:
git diff a1b2c3d..e4f5g6h

commonMistakes.text: `git diff` with no arguments shows UNSTAGED changes only. If you just ran `git add .`, the output will be empty even though files changed. Use `git diff --staged` to see staged changes.
For a visual diff tool instead of terminal output, configure one with `git config --global diff.tool vscode` and use `git difftool` instead of `git diff`.
The order matters in branch diffs. `git diff A..B` shows changes from A to B (what B has that A doesn't). Swap the order to see the reverse.
